newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Politicians gear up for final lap in Algiers poll.
newsitem.headline: Politicians gear up for final lap in Algiers poll.

text.p: Algeria's main political leaders moved into the last four campaigning days before next week's June 5 general election, focusing their sights on the big prize of Algiers and its 24 seats, and other main cities.

For the first time in Algeria's history, the main parties are confident under a new proportional representation system of gaining seats for their leaders, but were taking no chances in efforts to garner last minute support.

After criss-crossing the strife-ridden country during the past 16 days of campaigning, politicians were scrambling to gather backers in the big stadiums or movie theatres of the capital, home to an estimated three to four million people.
"As a result, Algiers has become all of a sudden too small to seat all this campaigning activity," wrote the evening daily Le Soir d'Algerie on Friday.

The Islamist-oriented Nahda party leader Abdallah Djaballah and other contending party officials said they had applied for the 20,000-seat Harcha indoor stadium but had been turned down because other parties had reserved it.

The secular Socialist Forces Front (FFS), one of 39 parties competing for the 380-seat lower house, on Friday was rallying supporters at the Harcha stadium to hammer home its message on the need for peace negotiations between opposition and the government to end Algeria's five years of violence.

"We had wanted the elections not to be held at this time because the urgent priority is peace. We are taking part in the poll to continue the democratic struggle and impose peace," said FFS leader Mustapha Bouhadef.
The rival Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD) party holds a campaign meeting some metres (yards) away to repeat its messages condemning both government and radical Islamists.
About 60,000 people have been killed since the authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election in which the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken a huge lead.

During campaigning, villagers have urged candidates to arm them against Moslem rebels blamed for massacres like one in which 93 people died in one community on the eve of the start of campaigning on May 15. Most had their throats cut.
Mohamed Salami, 23 and unemployed, said he and his fellow villagers at Ben Achour mountain hamlet near Blida, 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers, wanted weapons to defend families.

"We need heavy weapons or at least Kalashnikovs. Our village suffered from the terrorists who killed 19 people in the village eight months ago and 16 more 20 days later," he said adding that they now are armed with shotguns.

Many among the 1,200 families in Ben Achour village flocked on Thursday to Hamoud Daidi stadium in Blida to support the National Democratic Rally (RND) party which groups President Liamine Zeroual's backers.
Ahmed Dehmani, 41, said he and 220 villagers took arms to defend their hamlet. "All our village will vote for the RND."

FFS chief Hocine Ait Ahmed, who lives in self-exile abroad, joined other secularists in warning voters over what he saw as a threat to democracy from the main legal Islamist-leaning Movement for a Peaceful Society, formerly known as Hamas.
He said: "Hamas is more dangerous than the FIS because it is in a position to infiltrate the state in order to prepare a situation like Sudan", where Islamists dominate Khartoum's government.
Nahda's Djaballah played down any Islamist threat.
"The new constitution gives the president main powers and the current proportional voting system prevents any party from dominating the parliament," he told a news conference.

At rallies attended by thousands, voters in the oil and gas producing North African country's crowded cities and shantytowns told candidates they just wanted to live normal lives, free of violence, assured of justice, jobs and peace.
"Our main concern is job," shouted a young man to Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia campaigning in the decrepit Bourouba neihgbourhood in Algiers.
Algeria has more than two million unemployed among its 29 million people, most of them young.

"I will not promise you to resolve the jobless and housing crisis in some months or one year but I promise you that we will be just in resolving these problems," replied Ouyahia, a candidate for the National Democratic Rally.
